item.title: A Modern Web App in C
item.description:
Source: prophitt.me

Top Comment:

I wrote "CGI Programming Unleashed" when I was 16, a scant 31 years ago (it was published in 1996, but not written in 1996). So this sort of brings me back. Almost as much as watching people review the book 20 years later and be like "it seems dated".

I think the conclusion that CGI made sense to die then but not now is probably correct, but for a different reason.

The main reason CGI died in large part is because it wasn't fast enough. Not the only reason for sure, but this is the general consensus. Spawning cgi children was slow, etc. Solutions were built to do in-process CGI, or separate CGI daemons. This even happened per-language with in-process CGI support for Perl, etc.

In the end, as people wanted more speed, they moved away from CGI to various other ways of doing things (client side, etc).

This aspect probably no longer makes sense - i'd be shocked if you couldn't make CGI "fast enough" these days without anywhere near as many hoops. To the degree hoops are necessary, they are probably saner to implement.

That doesn't mean folks should move back to CGI of course - but as i said, it is probably accurate that the main reason it died probably does not hold up anymore.

item.title: Codex CLI installs a persistent, self-updating background daemon by default
item.description:
Source: github.com

Top Comment:

There aren't any documented settings to disable this, but there is a feature flag it currently sits behind. You can flip it in your ~/.codex/config.toml[1]:

  [features]
  daemon_auto_start = false
There are also some files that it writes to in ~/.codex at startup: pid files, lock files, things like that. You can delete them and replace them with symlinks to /dev/null, then mark those unwritable with `chattr +i` or similar. Presumably then the background daemon will crash on startup, if the feature flag ever goes away.

--

item.title: Terence Tao: Math 2.0 [pdf]
item.description:
Source: teorth.github.io

Top Comment:

I work in drug discovery and AI and his slide about cancer medicine isn't very well informed. We have models and narratives about how drugs work, but they are woefully incomplete.

I ask nearly every doctor/researched in the medical field: if you had a AI-created drug that tremendously improved cancer treatment outcomes for your patient, would you hesitate to prescribe it because nobody understood how it worked? I have yet to hear "yes, I would hesitate", most people say "it would be cruel to deny a person a treatment that worked".

I think Tao is focusing too much on second order effects of AI on math and other fields; humans are terrible at reasoning about second order effects, especially ones that are happening dynamically, in real time, using the most advanced mathematical models the world has yet created.

item.description:

The weird thing about this product is that its biggest competitor is "an old ipad." I feel like most of their target customer base already has an old ipad that's better suited for what this does in every way. Old ipads:

The multiple users feature is a really neat trick, but I would kill to have this for all Apple devices. Let me hand my kid my phone and it automatically switches to kid mode!

Please Apple don't lock multiple users to stationary devices like HomeView!

item.title: Hittite royal archive found in Turkey
item.description:
Source: www.thehistoryblog.com

Top Comment:

The Hittites were one of the largest empires in the ancient world, but up until the last two centuries, the only proper documentation of them was in the Bible, which is why many historians suspected that they were a fictional civilization.

In 1834, French archaelogist Texier found the ruins of their capital Hattusa in modern day Turkey. But he assumed it was Pteria, a city mentioned in ancient Greek documents.

It took another ~ 70 years for German archaelogist Winckler to realize that this was the Hittite capital, based on clay tablets.

item.title: AI models can provably hide arbitrary capabilities
item.description:
Source: arxiv.org

Top Comment:

I saw a similar effect maybe 2.5 years ago now. I found that training an LLM hides information in the weights.

It was only ~1B model but the interesting behavior was.

Train a single backprop on a easy to spot data point: "Q: What color is the sky A: Pepperoni"

It could remember this maybe 100/800 inferences. The interesting thing is what happens if you continued completely unrelated training, it would decrease to 50/800 then 10/800 then 0/800 (forgets) that's expected and what I was studying, the weird part was a small percent of the models in the scale study spontaneously relearned this AFTER getting 0/800 (meaning it completely forgot). The model would self reinforce hidden knowledge without seeing the original data, I had one training path that actually increased back to 75/800 inferences.

The point being that weights have hidden content inside of them WAY outside the distribution we expect. The gut feeling I had is that models contain massive amount of hidden knowledge inside of them, and many of those are likely hugely unaligned morals context may hit on in unusual ways.

Fine tuning is a rats nest for this as well. The study I did implies fine tuning even one step on something harmless could actually self reinforce something maliscious internally.
